conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your hospitalist during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been vomiting and having diarrhea—up to 15 times a day. And now there’s bright red blood in my stool, just small amounts, but it’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this started after a recent cautery procedure for ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about two weeks ago. I had bleeding ulcers in the jejunum and colon, and they cauterized them. Since then, I’ve had nausea and muddy stools, but no blood—until a couple days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers, dizziness, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. But I’m more tired than usual, and the pain is worse. My medical marijuana isn’t helping like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve checked your labs. Your hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL, which is low, and it’s been dropping over the past few weeks. That’s likely why you’re feeling fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been dropping? That’s not good. I was already anemic last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your iron and ferritin are very low. We’re concerned about ongoing blood loss. We’ll hold off on transfusion for now and try an IV iron infusion to see if we can stabilize you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but if I keep losing blood, will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But because of rare antibodies in your blood, we have to be careful with matching. We’ll monitor closely and only transfuse if absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s always complicated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve also ordered stool tests to rule out infections like C. diff, Salmonella, or parasites, since you have diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been on antibiotics lately, and no one around me is sick. I don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, we need to check. Your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and multiple surgeries makes your gut more vulnerable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the abdominal pain? Can I get something stronger? Dilaudid helps, but I get sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to balance pain control with safety. You do get quite somnolent with IV Dilaudid, so we’re limiting doses and using alternatives like acetaminophen when we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but the pain is really bad. I’ve been through 23 surgeries—this is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll keep adjusting. For now, let’s focus on finding the source of the bleeding. We’ve scheduled a flexible sigmoidoscopy for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us where the blood is coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will check the lower part of your colon and rectum. If we don’t find anything, we may need a deeper procedure like a double balloon enteroscopy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to stop losing blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back—all negative. No C. diff, no parasites, no bacterial infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection. That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good. It means we can focus on structural or vascular causes. Your abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops, mostly colonic, but no signs of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time. So it’s probably not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re still waiting for the iron infusion results. Your hemoglobin was 7.4 on admission, and we’re watching for any further drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on the pain meds? I’m still hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing with scheduled gabapentin and acetaminophen. We can give small doses of Dilaudid, but we’ll monitor your alertness closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you had the flexible sigmoidoscopy this morning. I have the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did they find the bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rectal ulcers from before have healed. The mucosa looks normal. There were a few small spots of old blood, possibly from rectal prolapse, but no active bleeding source was seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they don’t know where the blood came from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from this test. Since the bleeding was small volume and has slowed, and your hemoglobin stabilized for a bit, we proceeded with an IV iron infusion yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my counts kept dropping, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. After the iron, your hemoglobin continued to fall, so we decided to transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do with it? Any reaction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated it well. No signs of transfusion reaction. Your latest hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL, which is an improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So I’m not actively bleeding now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of active bleeding. The GI team thinks the bleed may have been self-limited, possibly from a small vessel or ulcer higher up that we couldn’t see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor. They may recommend a capsule endoscopy to look deeper into the small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? It’s better but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your pain regimen the same—gabapentin, rabeprazole, sucralfate, and as needed loperamide for diarrhea. We’ll avoid increasing opioids due to sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just want to feel more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more update—your labs this morning are stable. Hemoglobin is holding at 9.0. No further transfusion needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Make sure to see your primary doctor soon to check your blood counts again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I see more blood, I’ll come right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.
